title: Ruy Lopez: each side's setup and what each move prepares
outcomes: Says what Re1, Bb3, c3 and h3 each make possible in the Closed Ruy Lopez
Counts defenders and attackers of e4 and e5 as the set-up moves arrive
Explains why Black's regroup (Nb8-d7, Bb7, Re8, Bf8) is not wasted time
Compares the move orders 7...d6 and 7...O-O and says what each allows
Teaches the set-up to a beginner with the idea, when it works, an example and a warning

steps.caption: Ruy Lopez, White to move after 4...Nf6. The knight on f6 attacks the pawn on e4. Think of every way to deal with it, and what each one would help you do later. Nothing is explained yet.

claims.statement: The knight on f6 attacks the pawn on e4.
No white piece defends the pawn on e4.

steps.prompt: List the moves you would consider and, for each, one thing it makes possible later.

fields.label: My moves and what each prepares:

steps.text: **One question for every move.** [I] In a closed opening, ask of each early move: what does this make possible later? A move can free a piece, defend a pawn so another piece may leave, take a square away from the opponent, or prepare a lever. We go through White's set-up with that question, then Black's, then ask how the order of the moves matters.

**Castling does not defend e4.** [V] After 4...Nf6, masters castled in 10,556 games and played d3 in 1,414. [I] Castling puts the king in safety and the rook on f1. If Black takes e4, White regains the pawn with d4 and dxe5 (the Open Ruy Lopez). The calmer path is to defend e4 first. Both exist; the next board shows the most popular route.

steps.caption: Black has just played 5...Be7. Watch what 6.Re1 makes possible.

line.say: The rook goes behind the e4 pawn: it now defends the pawn, so the knight on f3 may move later.
Black grabs the pawn.
The rook takes the knight: Black has lost a piece for a pawn.

claims.statement: After Re1 the rook on e1 defends e4.
At depth 16 the position after Nxe4 Rxe4 is at least 250 centipawns in White's favour.

steps.text: **Re1 does two jobs.** It defends e4, so the knight on f3 is free to move, and it sits behind the e-pawn for a later advance of that pawn. [I] That is why the rook comes to e1 before the d-pawn moves. [V] After Black's bishop development, masters put the rook on e1 in 4,413 of 7,134 games and played d3 in 2,254 (counts of games, not evaluations).

steps.caption: Black pushes the queenside pawn at once. Where does the bishop live, and what does it do there?

line.say: The pawn attacks the bishop and gains space on the queenside.
The bishop retreats but keeps the diagonal toward f7.
Black supports e5 and opens the bishop on c8.

claims.statement: After b5 the pawn on b5 attacks the bishop on a4.
After Bb3 the bishop attacks the pawn on f7.
After Bb3 only the king defends f7.

steps.text: **Bb3, then c3 and h3.** [I] The bishop on b3 aims at f7, which Black must keep guarded. Next White plays c3, which does two jobs: it guards d4 for a later lever and empties c2, a retreat square for the bishop. Then h3 takes g4 away from Black's c8 bishop before d4 arrives. Each pawn move is a small step toward the centre lever, not a waiting move.

steps.caption: Two small pawn moves pay off. Step through and note which one each later move depends on.

line.say: White takes g4 away from the bishop on c8, so a later d4 will not be pinned by it.
Black attacks the bishop on b3.
The bishop uses the square the c3 pawn freed.
Black prepares the lever against d4.
White takes the centre: the c3 pawn already guards d4.

claims.statement: From the start the pawn on c3 guards d4.
After h3 the pawn on h3 attacks g4.
After Na5 the knight attacks the bishop on b3.
After Bc2 the bishop stands on c2.

steps.caption: Both sides finish their set-up. Notice that most of these moves change who defends e4 or e5.

line.say: The knight comes into play and defends e4.
Black attacks e4 with the bishop.
The bishop adds a third defender to e4.
The rook adds pressure on e4 and e5.
The knight starts its journey to g3.
The bishop leaves e7 and frees the rook's view of e5.
The knight defends e4 and eyes f5 and h5.
Black prepares to put the bishop on the long diagonal.

claims.statement: After Bb7 two black pieces attack e4.
After Bc2 three white pieces defend e4.
After Bf8 three black pieces defend e5.
After Ng3 the knight defends e4 together with the rook and the bishop.

steps.text: **White's set-up in one view.** [I] Re1 defends e4. Bb3 keeps the bishop alive and aims at f7. c3 guards d4 and empties c2. h3 asks Black's bishop a question before d4. Nbd2-f1-g3 reroutes the knight to a square where it defends e4 and eyes f5 and h5. Each early move earns a later one.

**Black asks the same question.** [I] ...a6 asks the bishop where it lives, ...Nf6 attacks e4, ...Be7 gets the bishop out of the way so Black can castle, ...b5 gains space with a tempo, ...d6 guards e5 and opens the bishop on c8. After castling, the pieces regroup behind the pawns: the knight to d7, the bishop to b7, the rook to e8, the other bishop back to f8.

steps.caption: Black's moves in this line, and what each prepares.

line.say: White defends e4.
Black attacks the bishop.
The bishop retreats.
Black guards e5 with a pawn and opens the bishop on c8.
White prepares the centre.
Black castles: the king is safe and the rook comes into play.

claims.statement: After d6 the pawn on d6 guards e5.
After d6 the bishop on c8 attacks a6, b7, d7, e6, f5, g4 and h3.
After O-O Black's king stands on the kingside.

steps.prompt: Black's bishop on c8 now sees g4. What would you expect White to do about that, and why?

steps.text: **Black's regroup.** [V] After White's h3, masters answered with the knight back to b8 in 640 games, the bishop to b7 in 590, the knight to a5 in 430 and the rook to e8 in 280. [I] The retreat sends the c6 knight toward d7, where it guards e5 and no longer blocks the c-pawn. The same knight has a second route: ...Na5 attacks the bishop and heads for c4. The bishop and rook pressure e4. These are different plans, not different moves.

steps.prompt: Name one move in Black's set-up that looks like it loses time but really adds a defender or an attacker.

steps.text: **Black's set-up in one view.** [I] ...a6 and ...b5 drive the bishop back. ...d6 guards e5 and opens the c8 bishop. The c6 knight re-centres by way of b8 and d7. The bishop on b7 hits e4. The rook on e8 and the bishop's retreat to f8 together put three defenders on e5. A later ...g6 prepares the long diagonal. Black's plan is to answer each White move with a move that keeps e5 safe and e4 under watch.

**What masters actually play.** Players reach similar positions by different routes, and each route allows something different. [V] After ...a6, masters retreated the bishop to a4 in 14,979 games and took on c6 in 608. After ...Nf6 they castled in 10,556, played d3 in 1,414, developed the b1 knight in 526, the queen in 101 and pushed d4 in 79 (counts of games, not evaluations). Sample: 329,379 master games.

steps.caption: The Exchange Variation: White trades the bishop for the knight. Compare with the main line: what does each side get?

line.say: White gives up the bishop at once, a different move order.
Black recaptures and gets doubled pawns on the c-file.
White castles.
Black pins the knight to the queen.
White asks the bishop a question.
Black keeps the pin by supporting the bishop.

claims.statement: After dxc6 Black has doubled pawns on c7 and c6.
After Bg4 the bishop on g4 attacks the knight on f3.
At depth 16 the position after ...h5 is between -30 and +50 centipawns for White.

steps.prompt: [H] The side that gives up the bishop pair gets a better pawn structure in return. Does this board support that, and what would you need to check?

steps.caption: Black castled before playing ...d6. This is the Marshall Attack: Black gives a pawn for active pieces. Watch what Black gets for the pawn.

line.say: Black castles at once and leaves d6 for later.
White prepares d4.
Black strikes in the centre with a pawn break.
White accepts the pawn.
Black recaptures and the knight is active.
White takes the pawn on e5.
Black takes the knight.
White takes back.
Black gives a pawn but opens lines for the bishops and the queen.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the position after ...c6 is between 0 and +80 centipawns for White, so the pawn is not lost for nothing.
After c3 the pawn on c3 guards d4.

steps.text: **What castling first allows.** [V] After Black castles on move seven, masters chose a4 in 978 games, c3 in 583, h3 in 362, d3 in 167 and d4 in 80. After c3, Black chose ...d5 in 350 of 579 games. [I] So castling first invites the ...d5 break, the Marshall Attack; playing ...d6 first does not. [H] White's popular a4 suggests that many players prefer to avoid it; the counts do not say.

steps.prompt: Name one thing these counts do not tell you about 7...O-O versus 7...d6. Think about who the players were and what they were choosing.

steps.caption: An answer to castling first: attack b5 with a4 and avoid the line with ...d5.

line.say: White attacks the b5 pawn at once and avoids the c3 and ...d5 line.
Black pushes past: the pawn will take on c3.
White offers the exchange of pawns.
Black takes.
White recaptures and the b-file opens.
Black finally supports e5.
White keeps the centre solid.
Black puts the rook on the open file.

claims.statement: After a4 the pawn on a4 attacks b5.
After bxc3 bxc3 the b-file is open.
At depth 16 the final position is between 0 and +60 centipawns for White.

steps.title: The same capture, one rook move apart
steps.prompt: Predict first: the knight on f6 captures on e4 in both positions. In the first, Black has played ...Be7 and White's rook stands on e1. In the second neither has happened: Black's bishop is still on f8 and White has only castled. In which one does the capture lose material?
Teach it back to a beginner who knows the rules, one box at a time: what Re1, c3 and h3 each make possible, why Black's retreat ...Bf8 is not wasted, when it works, an example and one warning.

fields.label: An example I could set up on a board:

steps.text: **Self-check.** Did you say what each move prepares (not only what it does now), give a reason for the order of the moves, give an example a beginner could set up, and name one mistake (for example capturing on e4 after Re1, or castling there and losing the e5 pawn to Bxc6 and Nxe5)? The app grades nothing; compare your answer with the points above.

**Recap.**
- Ask of every early move: what does it make possible later?
- Re1 defends e4 and frees the f3 knight.
- c3 guards d4 and empties c2.
- h3 takes g4 from the bishop.
- The d2 knight reaches g3 by f1.
- Black's retreat ...Bf8 adds a defender to e5.
- Move order decides which breaks the opponent gets.

steps.prompt: Which was least clear: what Re1 prepares, what c3 prepares, or why Black's pieces go back before they go forward? Write the position you would drill first as a move list or a FEN.
